clue.text: Establishment gains ground in formal speech

indicators.note: the reworked letters sit inside the speech word, splitting it after its first two letters

parts.note: an oration is a formal public address

indicators.note: ground as the past of grind: these letters have been milled into a new order

parts.note: the letters of gains are the raw material for the rearrangement

explanation.surface: An institution makes headway in a formal address.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground' reads as land being won, but it is the past tense of grind, signalling the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: An organisation is an institution or body, which is one sense of establishment.

clue.text: Maybe has a stronger navy than remote Aussies experienced with clippers?

definitions.text: Maybe has a stronger navy than

parts.note: out of the way, as in an out station
in Australian slang a gun is a top sheep-shearer

explanation.surface: Australian shearers are compared at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: In Australia and New Zealand a gun is an expert shearer; 'clippers' suggests fast sailing ships.
explanation.definitionFit: To outgun is to have more firepower than a rival, which a navy with more warships would.

clue.text: Long passage runs into kitchen

indicators.note: the abbreviation goes inside the kitchen word

parts.note: a galley is a ship's or plane's kitchen

explanation.surface: A long corridor leads into the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: R is the cricket abbreviation for runs.
explanation.definitionFit: A gallery can be a long corridor or covered walkway, as in a mine or a building.

clue.text: No name for a disciple who's out of favour?

definitions.note: the definition describes the person rather than naming them, hence the question mark

parts.note: taken as written
per, as in per annum, means for each
a son can be a follower, as in a son of the prophets

explanation.surface: No name is given for a follower who has fallen from grace.
explanation.walkthrough: A nonperson is someone officially ignored, as purged Soviet figures were.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonperson is someone treated as not existing because they have been disgraced or ostracised.

clue.text: Reel cut short following hoax

indicators.note: the reel word loses its final letter

parts.note: a reel for thread or film is a spool

explanation.surface: A truncated film reel follows a prank.
explanation.definitionFit: A spoof is a trick or parody meant to fool or amuse.

clue.text: Is successful in festival wearing this?

definitions.text: Is successful in festival wearing this?

indicators.note: the verb sits inside the festival's name

parts.note: Tet is the Vietnamese lunar new year festival
wins

explanation.surface: Someone triumphs at a festival in a matching knitwear set.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds the answer and the whole clue hints at the garment worn by a prize-winner.
explanation.definitionFit: A twinset is a matching jumper and cardigan worn together, a classic women's outfit.

clue.text: View ordinary wing

parts.note: a pinion is a bird's wing

explanation.surface: A plain opinion of a wing.
explanation.definitionFit: A view is a belief or judgement held on a matter, the same as an opinion.

clue.text: Potential of positions in Perth accepting one with boundless ability

indicators.note: the slang word takes the other letters into its middle

parts.note: possie is Australian slang for a position, and this Perth is in Western Australia

indicators.note: with its bounds removed, ability keeps only its inner letters

parts.note: the word ability minus its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Talent appears in a Scottish town's job openings.
explanation.walkthrough: Perth looks Scottish but is the Australian city, pointing to Aussie slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Possibilities are the prospects of what might happen or be done, so potential.

clue.text: Recurrence concerning vulgar episode surrounding clubs

parts.note: crude means coarse or rude

indicators.note: the episode word wraps around the card suit's abbreviation

parts.note: a scene is an incident or episode

explanation.surface: A vulgar incident at clubs keeps happening.
explanation.definitionFit: Recrudescence is the breaking out again of a disease or trouble after a dormant period.

clue.text: Delicacy consumed by visitor to Lancashire

indicators.note: the bird is eaten up by the following words, so it lies inside them

parts.note: the bird runs across the end of visitor, the word to and the start of Lancashire

explanation.surface: A tourist in Lancashire eats a local speciality.
explanation.walkthrough: The ortolan is a small bunting once eaten whole as a French delicacy, famously under a napkin.
explanation.definitionFit: The ortolan is a songbird prized by gourmets as a rare culinary treat.

clue.text: Put protective cover on steer I had oddly in shed

parts.note: a steer is a castrated bull, so an ox
contracted to I'd

indicators.note: only the first, third and fifth letters of the two words are kept

parts.note: the odd-numbered letters of these two words, counted together

explanation.surface: Someone protects a bullock they had kept in a shed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steer' looks like a verb but is the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: Oxidising forms an oxide layer, which on metals like aluminium shields the surface from further corrosion.

clue.text: Hug small cat, not completely unknown one finally

indicators.note: the cat word loses its last letter

parts.note: a queen is a female cat
algebra uses x, y and z for unknowns

indicators.note: only the last letter of one is taken

parts.note: the final letter of the word one

explanation.surface: Someone cuddles a little cat that is still partly a stranger.
explanation.walkthrough: A queen is the breeder's word for a female cat; Z is a standard mathematical unknown.
explanation.definitionFit: To squeeze someone is to embrace them tightly, a synonym of hug.

clue.text: Perhaps Bombay duck I essentially overdo is more difficult to swallow

parts.note: Bombay duck is not a bird but a small dried fish, so it is an example of a fish
taken as written

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its core, its two middle letters here

parts.note: the two letters at the centre of overdo

explanation.surface: Someone frets that overdoing the Bombay duck makes a dish harder to get down.
explanation.walkthrough: Bombay duck is a lizardfish eaten dried and salted in India; 'swallow' turns from eating to believing.
explanation.definitionFit: Fishy means suspicious, so a fishier story is less credible and harder to believe.

clue.text: Somewhat tipsy lad getting sick on vacation

indicators.note: the lad takes in the pair of letters, holding them inside

parts.note: a boy

indicators.note: the word is emptied, leaving just its outside letters

parts.note: the outside letters of sick once its middle is emptied

explanation.surface: A slightly drunk boy is ill while away on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On vacation' sounds like a holiday but means emptied of its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Bosky is old slang for slightly drunk, besides its usual sense of wooded.

clue.text: Working tradesmen polished

indicators.note: the letters are worked over and come out in a new order

parts.note: the letters of tradesmen supply the material for the new word

explanation.surface: Busy craftsmen give something a shine.
explanation.definitionFit: To smarten something is to tidy or spruce it up, making it look neat and refined.

clue.text: Classifying eccentric organists

indicators.note: the letters are put in an odd, unconventional order

parts.note: the letters of organists supply the material for the new word

explanation.surface: Odd organ players are being sorted into groups.
explanation.definitionFit: Assorting means arranging items into groups by type, as in sorting.

clue.text: Exceptionally sleazy nob's a layabout

indicators.note: the letters are arranged in an unusual way, unlike their normal order

parts.note: the letters of these words, without the possessive s, are the raw material

explanation.surface: An unusually seedy toff is idle.
explanation.walkthrough: A nob is British slang for a toff, someone upper class.
explanation.definitionFit: A lazybones is an idle person, the informal equivalent of a shirker or loafer.

clue.text: Lethargic people cross; doctor regularly overlooked disease

parts.note: a zo or dzo is a cross-breed of yak and cow

indicators.note: every other letter of disease is skipped

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of disease

explanation.surface: Someone angry finds a doctor kept missing an illness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like angry but is the yak hybrid; MB is a Bachelor of Medicine.
explanation.definitionFit: Zombies are informally people who move about listlessly, as if dead on their feet.

clue.text: Hatter, I believe, upset about religious headgear

indicators.note: in a down clue upset turns the letters upside down, so they read bottom to top
the hat sits about, spread around, the words of the clue

parts.note: the hat runs across the tail of Hatter, the word I and the start of believe

explanation.surface: A hatmaker voices doubts about a churchman's hat.
explanation.walkthrough: The hat is concealed backwards across hatter, I and believe.
explanation.definitionFit: A biretta is the square cap with ridges worn by Roman Catholic clergy.

clue.text: Juliet copies tricks

parts.note: J in the NATO phonetic alphabet
to ape is to imitate

explanation.surface: Juliet imitates someone's pranks.
explanation.definitionFit: Japes are practical jokes or pranks, the same as playful tricks.

clue.text: One's launched live broadcast in winter month

indicators.note: the rearranged letters sit inside the month abbreviation

parts.note: Jan is the short form of January

indicators.note: scattered about, so the letters of live are strewn into a new order

parts.note: the letters of live are scattered to form the middle

explanation.surface: A live broadcast goes out in January.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Launched' suggests a show starting; a javelin is thrown.
explanation.definitionFit: A javelin is the spear thrown in athletics, something hurled into the air.

clue.text: Help out remodelling gym in a stolid manner

definitions.note: an adverbial phrase for an adjective describing a phlegmatic, unexcitable temperament

indicators.note: the letters are out of their proper order

parts.note: the letters of help are rearranged for the first part

indicators.note: the gym word is reshaped into a new order

parts.note: the letters of gym are rearranged for the end

explanation.surface: Someone helps refit a gym, quite unmoved.
explanation.definitionFit: Phlegmy can mean phlegmatic, from the old humour phlegm thought to make people sluggish and calm.

clue.text: Revolutionary transport of corporation mostly excellent

parts.note: a jocular old word for a large belly

indicators.note: the slang word loses its final letter

parts.note: brill is British slang for brilliant

explanation.surface: A company's vehicle in the uprising was largely first-rate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corporation' is a humorous term for a paunch; a tumbril carried victims to the guillotine in the French Revolution.
explanation.definitionFit: A tumbril was the cart that took condemned prisoners to execution during the French Revolution.

clue.text: Give false impression, say, about subject

parts.note: to lie

indicators.note: the abbreviation is turned round

explanation.surface: Someone misleads, for example, regarding a subject.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Subject' looks like a topic but is a vassal; liege can mean the subject owing feudal service.
explanation.definitionFit: Liege can describe a vassal bound to serve a lord, so a feudal subject.

clue.text: Reassess Swiss mathematician making comeback involving volume and area

indicators.note: the turned name wraps around the two abbreviations
the name returns, so it is read from end to start

parts.note: Leonhard Euler, the eighteenth-century Swiss mathematician

explanation.surface: A Swiss mathematician returns to rethink his work on volume and area.
explanation.definitionFit: To revalue something is to set a new worth on it, so to appraise it afresh.

clue.text: Record first heartless love letter

parts.note: an EP is an extended-play record
1st, with the digit read as the letter I

indicators.note: the middle two letters are cut out, leaving only the outer pair

parts.note: the word love supplies its outer letters

explanation.surface: The first record of a lover's note lacks feeling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heartless' seems to describe the love letter but only strips the middle from love.
explanation.definitionFit: An epistle is a formal letter, as with the New Testament epistles.

clue.text: Lack of sense of sick old gaffer principally in charge

parts.note: to be sick is to be ill

indicators.note: only the leading letter of gaffer is used

parts.note: the first letter of gaffer, a British word for a boss

explanation.surface: An ailing elderly boss in charge talks nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: A gaffer is British slang for a boss or an old man.
explanation.definitionFit: Illogic is absence of reasoning, an irrationality of argument.

clue.text: Letters can get at eyes in a bad way

indicators.note: the letters are in poor shape, jumbled out of order

parts.note: these words supply the twelve letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Something can make the eyes sore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letters' are not alphabet characters but those who let property.
explanation.definitionFit: An estate agency lets houses and flats to tenants, so its staff are letting agents.
